content: Midwifery refers to the specialized practice of assisting women during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period. Modern midwives are healthcare professionals trained to provide comprehensive care to women, including prenatal care, labor and delivery support, and postnatal care for both the mother and infant. They are experts in managing normal pregnancies and births, emphasizing a natural and minimally invasive approach unless complications arise. Midwives are autonomous practitioners who collaborate with obstetricians when medical or surgical intervention is required. They are also trained to handle certain abnormal situations, such as breech births or posterior fetal positions, using non-invasive techniques. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines a midwife as a professional who has completed a recognized midwifery education program and is legally licensed to practice. They also play a vital role in health education, counseling, and preparation for parenthood, extending their expertise to areas such as sexual and reproductive health. Midwives can practice in various settings, including homes, communities, hospitals, and clinics. Historically, midwifery has been a female-dominated profession, with roots tracing back to ancient Greece. In the 18th century, a divide emerged between midwives and surgeons, as male medical practitioners began to assert the superiority of their scientific methods over traditional midwifery practices. Some historians suggest that midwives were targeted during the witch hunts in Europe due to their knowledge of contraception and abortion, which conflicted with efforts to repopulate the continent after the Black Death. This persecution may have contributed to the decline of midwifery and the rise of medicalized childbirth. In the United States, midwifery is divided into two main categories: nurse-midwives and direct-entry midwives. Nurse-midwives are advanced practice nurses with specialized training in obstetrics and gynecology. They often hold a master’s degree and are licensed to prescribe medications. Nurse-midwives typically work in hospitals, clinics, or private practices and may collaborate with obstetricians for high-risk pregnancies. Direct-entry midwives, on the other hand, are trained specifically in midwifery through various educational pathways, such as apprenticeships or midwifery schools, without requiring a nursing background. They primarily provide care in out-of-hospital settings, such as homes or birthing centers. In the United Kingdom, midwives are independent practitioners responsible for antenatal, intrapartum, and postnatal care. Most midwives qualify through a direct-entry university program, while others transition from nursing through additional training. Midwifery care is provided within the National Health Service (NHS) or through independent practice. Midwives advocate for natural childbirth and act as the primary caregivers during labor, ensuring that women retain control over their birthing experience. They are trained to recognize complications and refer cases to medical professionals when necessary. In Canada, midwifery became a regulated profession in the 1960s and is now integrated into the healthcare system in several provinces. Canadian midwives provide continuity of care, informed choice, and options for birthplace, including home, birthing centers, and hospitals. They are trained to manage normal pregnancies and consult with or transfer care to other healthcare providers when complications arise. Midwifery education in Canada typically involves a four-year university degree, and midwives are authorized to prescribe medications, order diagnostic tests, and provide comprehensive maternity care. In New Zealand, midwifery regained its status as an independent profession in 1990. Midwives provide care from early pregnancy to six weeks postpartum, focusing on normal pregnancies and births. Women can choose a midwife, general practitioner, or obstetrician for their maternity care, with the majority opting for midwives. Midwifery care is government-funded, and births can take place at home, in primary birthing units, or in hospitals. Midwives consult or transfer care to specialists when complications occur, ensuring safe and comprehensive care for mothers and infants.
